callouts.label: Elevator Shaft and Stairwell as Flues
callouts.hint: Find the two tall slim vertical shafts inside the building, one holding an elevator car and one holding a zigzag stair, running from the ground to the roof.
callouts.description: Elevator shafts and stairwells run most of the height of a tall building with few floors interrupting them. That makes them the easiest vertical paths for air, like the flue of a chimney. Air moves through them far more easily than through the walls and floors around them (Chapter 4).
callouts.tip: A shaft is a stack effect highway. Whatever is in the air at the bottom can be at the top within minutes.

callouts.label: Warm Air Escapes High
callouts.hint: Find the cluster of red arrows curling out through the roof edge and the top-floor windows.
callouts.description: In winter, warm indoor air is lighter than cold outdoor air, so it rises and leaks out through gaps near the top: roof-to-wall joints, upper windows, and penetrations. The taller the building and the colder the day, the harder it pushes (BSI-075; Chapter 4). It carries heat and indoor moisture outward with it.

callouts.label: Uneven Heating Between Floors
callouts.hint: Find the row of thermometers beside the building, with a red-filled one at the top floors and a blue-filled one at the bottom floors.
callouts.description: Rising warm air leaves at the top while cold air is pulled in at the bottom, so lower floors can feel cool and drafty while upper floors run warm. In multifamily buildings the air from lower units also ends up in upper units (BSI-075), carrying odors and moisture with it.
callouts.tip: Seal the top and the bottom of the enclosure and the shafts between them, not just the walls.

callouts.label: Summer Reverses the Flow
callouts.hint: Find the smaller building on the right with its arrows flipped: red arrows entering near the roof and blue arrows leaving at the base, under a bright sun.
callouts.description: In an air-conditioned building on a hot day, indoor air is cooler and denser than outdoor air, so the flow reverses: warm outdoor air leaks in high and cool indoor air leaks out low. BSI-075 notes the flow reverses in cooling seasons. The temperature difference is usually smaller than in winter, so the effect is usually weaker.

callouts.label: Smoke Drawn Toward the Stairwell
callouts.hint: Find the floor plan in the upper-right inset where a gray smoke cloud leaks through a corridor door toward a zigzag stair symbol.
callouts.description: In a tall building in cold weather, stack effect can pull smoke from a lower-floor fire into stairwells and elevator shafts and carry it to floors far above the fire. BSI-075 notes it can compromise smoke control and fire safety. A fire adds its own heat, so engineers analyze smoke movement for each building.
callouts.tip: A stairwell is an escape route only while it stays clear of smoke. Keep stair doors closed.

callouts.label: Cold Air Enters Low
callouts.hint: Find the cluster of blue arrows entering through the lobby doors and gaps near the ground on the left of the building.
callouts.description: Below the neutral pressure plane the building is at lower pressure than the outdoors, so cold air is drawn in through lobby doors, loading docks, leaks around the foundation, and the lowest windows. That cold air has to be heated, which is part of how stack effect raises energy bills (BSI-075; Chapter 4).

callouts.label: Doors That Slam or Stick
callouts.hint: Find the swinging entrance door at ground level with a curved motion line and a small arrow pushing it inward.
callouts.description: The pressure difference across a ground-level door is largest near the base of a tall building in winter. It can pull a door shut hard or make it difficult to open. Codes limit how much force an exit door may need to open, so designers control these pressures with vestibules and tight shafts.
callouts.tip: Revolving doors and vestibules add a second barrier so no single door takes the full pressure.

callouts.label: Whistling at the Elevator Lobby
callouts.hint: Find the lobby beside the shaft, with elevator doors slightly parted and wavy sound lines coming from a narrow gap.
callouts.description: Elevator doors and lobby partitions are not airtight, and the shaft behind them connects many floors. Air squeezed through narrow gaps at speed whistles and makes drafts that occupants notice. It is a sign that stack pressure is pushing air through the shaft, and a clue to where air sealing is needed.

callouts.label: Neutral Pressure Plane
callouts.hint: Find the dashed horizontal line across the building about halfway up, with small outward arrows above it and inward arrows below it.
callouts.description: The neutral pressure plane is the height where indoor and outdoor pressure are equal. Above it air flows out; below it air flows in (BSI-075; Chapter 4). Its height depends on where the leaks are in the enclosure and shafts, so it moves as the building is sealed or as doors and windows are opened.
callouts.tip: Think of it as the waterline of an air tank: pressure is positive above, negative below.

callouts.label: Pressurized Stair Keeps Smoke Out
callouts.hint: Find the floor plan in the lower-right inset where a fan sits at the base of a stair and green arrows push air outward through the closed door toward the corridor.
callouts.description: A smoke-control design can supply outdoor air to a stairwell so that its pressure is higher than the floors around it. Air then flows outward through gaps around closed doors and smoke is kept from flowing in. Engineers design and test these systems for each building and its code (Chapter 18).
